title: Orbit and Echo
premise: Kestrel Blackwood makes her living proving disasters are nobody's fault, until a distress signal in dead High Meridian arrives at the failing colony of Vesper's Reach, where she's documenting the slow collapse of a settlement the insurance consortium wrote off years ago. The signal is a dying admiral's confession: the war's founding atrocity was staged, and the proof is encoded in Kestrel's own inherited memory implant, a legacy from the mother who abandoned her. Hunted by a consortium enforcer who was once her partner, and sheltered by the ragtag colonists who become the family she never had, Kestrel must decide whether broadcasting the truth will save Vesper's Reach or paint a target on it. She broadcasts it — and in the aftermath, chooses the colony over her career, delivering the message that ends the war at the cost of everything she was.
about_author: Edmund Ishikawa is a former marine salvage auditor who spent a decade inspecting derelict stations before turning to fiction. He writes in a converted cargo pod docked at a decommissioned orbital yard, where he claims the vacuum silence improves his prose.

chapters.title: Actuarial Grace
chapters.summary: Kestrel arrives at Vesper's Reach to close its final insurance file, cataloguing a colony dying of neglect. Through her detached POV we meet innkeeper Sefa and her adopted crew of strays. Beat: professional coldness cracking at the edges as Kestral realizes she's writing an obituary, not a report.

chapters.title: The Language of the Dead
chapters.summary: A signal hits the colony's ancient receiver: fluent High Meridian, extinct for two centuries. Kestrel's inherited implant translates it before she chooses to. Beat: dread and wonder as the dead speak, and the colony's forgotten comms officer, Idris, becomes suddenly important.

chapters.title: Inventory of Strays
chapters.summary: Kestrel interviews the colonists to trace the signal's origin, and their stories — a deserter, a disgraced medic, a child born in transit — mirror her own orphaned history. Beat: reluctant belonging; she starts lying to her consortium handlers to protect them.

chapters.title: What the Implant Remembers
chapters.summary: The implant surfaces fragments of Kestrel's mother's naval service: coordinates, a code phrase, a name — Admiral Voss. Kestrel decodes a partial confession hidden in the signal. Beat: betrayal; the mother she mourned was a war criminal's witness, not a deserter.

chapters.title: The Man from Claims
chapters.summary: Consortium enforcer Dax Renn arrives — Kestrel's former partner — ostensibly to audit her expense accounts, actually to silence the signal. Beat: old loyalty weaponized; their dinner conversation is a duel conducted in courtesy.

chapters.title: Sefa's Table
chapters.summary: A quiet chapter: the colony shares a harvest-poor feast, and Sefa tells Kestrel why she never left. Idris confesses he's been receiving the signal for months and hiding it. Beat: found family crystallizes; Kestrel is given a seat she didn't ask for.

chapters.title: Voss's Ghost
chapters.summary: Following the implant's coordinates, Kestrel and Idris find a wreck in the system's dust belt: Admiral Voss's flagship, intact, its logs still sealed. Beat: awe curdling to horror as the first log plays — footage of the atrocity that started the war, staged.

chapters.title: Chain of Custody
chapters.summary: Kestrel documents the wreck with an investigator's precision, building an evidence chain no court could dismiss. Dax's shuttle shadows them. Beat: purpose replacing fear; her old profession becomes her weapon.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Dax corners Kestrel: the consortium will bury the truth and pay her a fortune, or bury her with it. He reveals her mother sold the implant's existence to save infant Kestrel's life. Beat: the loyalty-vs-truth fault line opens; she refuses, and he lets her go — once.

chapters.title: Blackout at Vesper's Reach
chapters.summary: The consortium cuts the colony's power and traffic lanes, a slow strangulation disguised as bureaucracy. Sefa organizes rationing; the colonists choose to stay. Beat: solidarity under siege; Kestrel stops being an observer and becomes a resident.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: The signal resumes — a live transmission now. Someone aboard the wreck is awake: Voss's last crewman, cryo-suspended for two hundred years, completing his admiral's dead-man's broadcast. Beat: hope and urgency; the message needs a relay only Vesper's Reach can provide.

chapters.title: Terms of Inheritance
chapters.summary: Kestrel learns her mother didn't abandon her — she hid the implant in her daughter as the only vault the consortium couldn't search. The final key is a memory Kestrel has carried since childhood without understanding. Beat: grief transmuted into inheritance; she accepts the legacy.

chapters.title: What Dax Owes
chapters.summary: Dax's POV: his own file on Kestrel's mother, the debt he owes the consortium, and the moment he falsified his first report for her years ago. Beat: his loyalty inverts; he begins feeding her the consortium's timetable under cover of his audit.

chapters.title: The Relay Problem
chapters.summary: Broadcasting the confession requires the colony's decommissioned deep-space array, which needs a component only the consortium depot holds. Idris proposes theft; Sefa proposes asking. Beat: the family debates its soul — and chooses to ask first, steal second.

chapters.title: Depot Run
chapters.summary: Kestrel, Idris, and the deserter pilot Juno infiltrate the consortium depot using Kestrel's own credentials. Dax covers their exit and burns his career doing it. Beat: trust as a leap; the enemy becomes an ally mid-firefight.

chapters.title: Countdown to Silence
chapters.summary: The consortium dispatches a navy cutter with orders to erase Vesper's Reach and the wreck. Kestrel calculates they have forty hours. The colonists vote — overwhelmingly — to broadcast. Beat: terror and resolve; the forgotten colony claims its own name.

chapters.title: The Admiral's Last Order
chapters.summary: Aboard the wreck, the awakened crewman, Ensign Rao, gives Kestrel the final cipher — and his own testimony. The implant unlocks fully. Beat: the weight of two centuries of silence ending; Kestrel weeps for the first time in the book.

chapters.title: Forty Hours
chapters.summary: The colony rebuilds the array in an impossible sprint — every stray contributing a skill, Kestrel coordinating with an investigator's rigor. Dax feeds false positions to the cutter. Beat: communal triumph; the found family functions as one organism.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: The confession goes out on every band, in High Meridian and the trade tongue, signed with Kestrel's mother's name and Kestrel's own. The cutter arrives as the transmission completes. Beat: catharsis at maximum cost; there is no taking it back.

chapters.title: The War That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Both fleets receive the truth; the cutter's captain, herself a colonist's daughter, stands down. Ceasefire spreads faster than the consortium can suppress it. Beat: stunned peace; Dax surrenders his files and chooses the colony's side in the inquiry to come.

chapters.title: Claims Adjusted
chapters.summary: The consortium collapses into scandal; Vesper's Reach's insurance file is reopened as a restoration grant. Kestrel formally resigns, tearing up the report that would have closed the colony forever. Beat: justice with texture; the dead are named and mourned.

chapters.title: Orbit and Echo
chapters.summary: A year later: the colony thrives, Rao plants Voss's flag as a memorial, and Kestrel — resident, not investigator — teaches the colony's children to read the old language. The final echo of the signal plays on the receiver, kept deliberately unrepaired. Beat: belonging; the message delivered was hers all along.
